result.summary: This PR raises the minimum C++ language standard from C++20 to C++23 across CMake, depends, and CI configurations, bumping the minimum compiler requirements to GCC 13 and Clang 19. It removes in-tree polyfills like util::Expected, custom byteswap wrappers, and the ALWAYS_FALSE type workaround in favor of std::expected, std::byteswap, and static_assert(false). It also applies C++23 standard library features across the codebase, including std::views::zip and .contains() for string and container lookups.
result.problem: Maintaining compatibility with C++20 forces developers to keep in-tree polyfills and workarounds, prevents the use of modern standard library utilities, and conflicts with dependencies like libmultiprocess that have already started adopting C++23 features.
evidence: Author notes in the description that "workarounds to avoid C++23 keep accumulating and some parts of the code already use C++23 features, such as lambda attributes (libmultiprocess@bdd0cd6)", and that this switch is needed so that "new stuff is unlocked", referencing discussion in #34979.
result.scope_notes: Touches build configuration and over 50 files across the codebase, mostly performing mechanical replacements of std::string::find with .contains() alongside replacing util::Expected with std::expected.
result.changed_since_previous: Added header includes across multiple source files to satisfy Include-What-You-Use (IWYU) re-export heuristics with C++23 stdlib headers.
result.card: This PR raises the minimum required C++ standard to C++23 across CMake, depends, and CI, raising minimum compiler versions to GCC 13 and Clang 19. It replaces custom in-tree polyfills such as util::Expected and byteswap macros with std::expected and std::byteswap, and adopts C++23 features like .contains() and std::views::zip across the tree. The author notes that workarounds avoiding C++23 continue to accumulate while dependencies like libmultiprocess already use C++23 features. This draft RFC is intended to unblock further C++23 modernization tracked in #34979.

risk.why: Raising compiler requirements can break builds on older toolchains and supported platforms or expose standard library bugs across different C++23 implementations.
